name: New York City
scope: The world city on the island of Manhattan, at the mouth of the Hudson. T1: the Statue of Liberty is made of thin COPPER (about the thickness of two pennies) and started shiny brown — the famous green is a weathered copper patina, not paint. T1: Central Park is a rectangle of 843 acres dropped into mid-Manhattan and is entirely LANDSCAPED — the 'natural' park is the most man-made thing in the city (Olmsted & Vaux's 1858 Greensward Plan; millions of cubic feet of rock moved, topsoil trucked in). T2: the Brooklyn Bridge (opened 1883) was the world's LONGEST suspension bridge and among the first strung from steel wire; its towers were sunk on caissons where workers got 'the bends' — John Roebling died before it began, his son Washington was crippled by caisson disease, and Emily Roebling finished it. T2: Grand Central Terminal's turquoise ceiling shows the zodiac painted BACKWARDS (east where west should be), and a single dark patch was left uncleaned to show decades of tobacco grime. T3: Manhattan's numbered street GRID was drawn by the Commissioners' Plan of 1811 before the city reached there; the one great diagonal, Broadway, follows an old Native American trail and slices the grid into triangular 'squares' — Times, Herald, Madison. T3: Grand Central has 44 PLATFORMS and 67 tracks, more than any station on Earth. T4: the skyscrapers stand on hard bedrock called Manhattan SCHIST; the island's name comes from the Lenape 'Mannahatta,' island of many hills. T4: the Hudson beside Manhattan is really a tidal ESTUARY, an arm of the sea that reverses with the tides — the Lenape called it 'the river that flows both ways.' T5: the Empire State Building (1931) rose in about 410 days during the Depression, was the world's tallest for ~40 years, and its spire was designed as an airship mooring mast. T5: almost all the city's water arrives by GRAVITY alone through tunnels from Catskill reservoirs 100+ miles away, with no pumps.
source: Wikipedia: Grand Central Terminal (44 platforms/67 tracks, opened 1913), Grand Central Terminal art + Untapped New York + Artnet (reversed zodiac, Cancer soot-patch left uncleaned), Central Park (843 acres, Greensward Plan, entirely landscaped, sunken transverse roads, most-visited US park), Brooklyn Bridge (1883, longest suspension span at opening, Roebling family, caisson disease). Build stage: corroborate on Grokipedia first (blocked to fetch tool here); verify Statue of Liberty copper patina, Manhattan schist, Hudson tidal-estuary Lenape name, Empire State 410-day build + mooring mast, Catskill gravity aqueduct.
framing_note: Wonder voice: each rung's answer is the single most memorable specific fact, and every stem names NYC or a named NYC landmark; every answer is a place/structure fact (a named building, a landform, a design move), never a bare person or date. Invert the wonder — put the superlative in the stem ('the longest bridge in the world in 1883' -> the Brooklyn Bridge). Accuracy rail: the Statue of Liberty's green is copper patina (not bronze, not paint); the reversed ceiling is documented but the WHY (working from a flat sketch projected upward) is a leading explanation, so attribute it, don't assert it. Dinner-test payoff: the backwards zodiac ceiling and the Hudson that flows both ways. Lane border: Ellis Island immigration = history bank, Broadway shows/pizza = other banks — keep answers to the PLACE and its structures.

name: Chicago
scope: The flat city on Lake Michigan, birthplace of the skyscraper. T1: the Home Insurance Building (1885), by William Le Baron Jenney, is widely credited as the world's first SKYSCRAPER — the first tall building held up by an internal steel/iron skeleton instead of thick stone walls, so the outer walls could hang like curtains. T1: the whole downtown was physically JACKED UP out of the mud in the 1850s-60s on thousands of screw-jacks to fit sewers underneath — hotels were lifted while guests stayed inside; young George Pullman ran crews of 600 men turning 6,000 jackscrews. T2: engineers REVERSED the Chicago River in 1900 so the city's sewage would flow away from Lake Michigan (its drinking water) toward the Mississippi, by digging the Sanitary and Ship Canal. T2: the elevated railway that circles downtown, 'the L,' gives the business district its name — 'the Loop.' T3: the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 burned the wooden city, and the rebuild drew the architects who invented steel-frame design — the disaster is why the 'Chicago School' of architecture was born there. T3: the lakefront is kept 'forever open, clear and free' as public park, not private towers, thanks to Aaron Montgomery Ward's lawsuits and the 1909 Burnham Plan. T4: the Willis (Sears) Tower, 1973, at 1,451 ft was the world's tallest building for ~25 years, built as nine square 'bundled tubes' strapped together. T4: Chicago is famously FLAT because it sits on the bed of a vanished ice-age lake (glacial Lake Chicago) — the flatness is a fossil lakebed. T5: the low, swampy Chicago Portage — a natural divide where canoes crossed between the Great Lakes and Mississippi watersheds — runs right through the city and is the reason the city exists here. T5: to keep storm water out of the lake, Chicago dug the 'Deep Tunnel' (TARP) hundreds of feet down, one of the largest civil-engineering works in the world.
source: Wikipedia: Home Insurance Building ('often cited as the world's first skyscraper,' Jenney, 1885, steel skeleton, 10->12 stories), Raising of Chicago (Chesbrough 1856 sewer plan, jackscrews, George Pullman, Tremont House lifted with guests inside) corroborated via Enjoy Illinois + Gizmodo, Chicago River (1900 reversal, Sanitary and Ship Canal). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here); verify Willis Tower height/bundled-tube + tallest-until-1998, glacial Lake Chicago flatness, Chicago Portage watershed divide, Burnham Plan / lakefront-public, Deep Tunnel/TARP scale.
framing_note: Wonder voice: every stem names Chicago or a named Chicago place; every answer is a place/engineering fact (a named building, the reversed river, the raised streets), never a bare person or date. Invert the wonder — the hook is the impossible-sounding feat, the answer is the concrete thing. Accuracy rail: say the Home Insurance Building is 'widely credited' as the first skyscraper (the claim is genuinely debated); the reversal opened Jan 1900. Dinner-test payoff: raising the whole city on jackscrews, and reversing a river's flow. Lane border: deep-dish/Chicago hot dog = cooking bank (one-line mention only, never a food ladder).
history_overlap: The Great Chicago Fire (1871) is a candidate history-bank episode; this ladder uses it only as setup and keeps the answer the architectural rebirth (a place-fact), so no full-episode duplication — flag if the history bank also ladders the fire itself.

name: Mexico City (Tenochtitlan)
scope: The vast capital in a mountain-ringed basin, built where the Aztec island-city stood. T1: Mexico City sits atop Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital founded in 1325 on an ISLAND in Lake Texcoco and reached by long causeways — an engineered water-city bigger than most European capitals of its day. T1: the Aztecs farmed on chinampas, 'floating gardens' built up from the lakebed; the canals of Xochimilco are the last living piece of that lake-city. T2: the Spanish drained the lake, and now the city is SINKING — parts drop nearly 50 cm a year as the old lakebed clay dries and compacts, up to 9 m of sinking in a century. T2: you can watch it sink — the Metropolitan Cathedral tilts on an uneven foundation and the Angel of Independence column had extra steps added at its base as the ground fell away. T3: in 1978 electric-company workers digging downtown struck a giant carved stone disk of the dismembered goddess Coyolxauhqui — they had found the Templo Mayor, the Aztec great temple, buried under the modern streets. T3: the Zocalo, one of the largest city squares on Earth, sits directly on that buried Aztec ceremonial center. T3: Chapultepec is a forested hill crowned by a castle, with a park bigger than New York's Central Park inside the city; the Nahuatl name means 'grasshopper hill.' T4: the city stands at 2,240 m (7,350 ft) in a bowl ringed by mountains — the Valley of Mexico is ENDORHEIC (no natural river out), which is why floods and drainage have plagued it for 500 years. T4: two snow-capped volcanoes, active Popocatepetl ('the smoking mountain') and Iztaccihuatl, loom over the valley. T5: the soft old lakebed clay traps and AMPLIFIES earthquake waves, so the 1985 and 2017 quakes centered far away still shook the city violently — the ground rings like jelly. T5: to drain the closed basin, engineers cut the Tajo de Nochistongo and later the giant Tunel Emisor tunnels through the mountains — a 400-year fight to move water out.
source: Wikipedia: Mexico City (Tenochtitlan founded 1325 on Lake Texcoco island, altitude 2,240 m, subsidence ~50 cm/yr and up to 9 m, endorheic Valley of Mexico, 1985 quake, 17th-c drainage works), Templo Mayor (Feb 1978 CFE electrical workers, Coyolxauhqui monolith, Matos Moctezuma excavations). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here); verify Xochimilco chinampas as lake-city remnant, Metropolitan Cathedral tilt + Angel-of-Independence added steps, Zocalo size ranking, Chapultepec vs Central Park size + 'grasshopper hill,' Popocatepetl activity, lakebed seismic amplification in 1985/2017, Tunel Emisor drainage.
framing_note: Stance: celebrate Tenochtitlan as a FULL engineered civilization (causeways, chinampas, aqueducts, a metropolis larger than most European capitals) — never 'primitive' or 'exotic.' Every stem names Mexico City / Tenochtitlan / a named site; every answer is a place-fact. Accuracy rail: 1325 founding, ~50 cm/yr subsidence, and the 1978 Templo Mayor discovery are documented; the Popocatepetl/Iztaccihuatl warrior-and-lover story is Aztec LEGEND — flag it as legend, and the answer is the volcanoes, not the tale. Dinner-test payoff: the sinking city, and the Aztec great temple unearthed by utility workers. Lane border: Xochimilco's axolotl biology = animal bank (keep the answer the canals/chinampas, the PLACE); Mexican cuisine = cooking bank.
history_overlap: The 1521 Spanish conquest is a history-bank episode; this ladder deliberately avoids it, anchoring every answer to the place (the drained lake, the buried ruins, the sinking) — keep it that way.

name: San Francisco
scope: The foggy peninsula city on hills above a great bay. T1: the Golden Gate Bridge is painted 'International Orange,' a warm red-orange chosen by architect Irving Morrow so it glows against fog and blue water — the Navy had wanted black-and-yellow stripes. T1: 'Golden Gate' is not the bridge but the narrow STRAIT it crosses, named by explorer John C. Fremont before any bridge existed. T2: San Francisco runs the last manually operated CABLE-CAR system on Earth — engineless cars that grip a moving underground cable to climb the hills (Andrew Hallidie, 1873). T2: for over 200 years Spanish ships sailed right past the Golden Gate without noticing the huge bay behind it — fog and the narrow gap hid it; it was finally found in 1769 by Portola's LAND expedition stumbling onto it from the hills. T3: the summer fog is 'advection fog' — warm inland air pulls in ocean air chilled by the cold California Current welling up offshore, and the fog pours through the Golden Gate like a river. T3: Alcatraz island sits in water so cold and currents so strong that its federal prison (1934-63) barely needed a sea wall — the bay itself was the cage. T4: the San Andreas Fault runs just offshore, and in 1906 its rupture plus three days of FIRE destroyed most of the city — the fire, not the shaking, did the worst. T4: in the 1989 Loma Prieta quake the Marina District shook hardest because it is built on landfill that turned to liquid ('LIQUEFACTION') while bedrock nearby held firm. T5: San Francisco Bay is the largest ESTUARY on the Pacific coast of the Americas — most of the Sierra Nevada's snowmelt drains to the sea through this one gap. T5: Lombard Street's eight switchback curves exist because the natural hill is too steep (27 degrees) for cars to climb straight — the crookedness is an engineering fix, not a gimmick.
source: Wikipedia: Cable car (railway) ('the only known existing traditional cable car system is San Francisco... manually operated,' Hallidie 1873, Clay Street Hill Railroad). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here) then Wikipedia: Golden Gate Bridge (International Orange, Irving Morrow), Golden Gate (strait, Fremont naming), San Francisco Bay + Portola expedition (1769 land sighting, ships passing the fog-hidden strait), San Francisco fog (advection fog + California Current), Alcatraz, 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire + San Andreas Fault, 1989 Loma Prieta + Marina liquefaction, Lombard Street.
framing_note: Wonder voice: every stem names San Francisco or a named SF place; every answer is a place-fact (a named landmark, a strait, an earth-process). Accuracy rail: teach 'advection fog' and 'liquefaction' before testing them; International Orange was Morrow's choice; the bay-hidden-for-200-years is documented (repeated Spanish voyages missed the fog-shrouded strait). Dinner-test payoff: the giant bay explorers missed for two centuries, and the only surviving cable-car system. Lane border: Pier 39 sea lions = animal bank; sourdough = cooking bank — keep answers to the PLACE.

name: New Orleans
scope: The crescent city in the Mississippi delta, mostly below sea level. T1: most of New Orleans sits in a BOWL below sea level — the Mississippi on one side runs higher than the streets, held back by levees; without pumps the city would flood on a sunny day. T1: the oldest part, the French Quarter (Vieux Carre), was built on the natural river LEVEE — the highest ground — so it stayed mostly dry in Hurricane Katrina while newer, lower neighborhoods flooded. T2: New Orleans buries its dead ABOVE ground in stone tombs — whole 'Cities of the Dead' — the reason locals give is a water table so high that coffins once floated up out of the earth. T2: the city curves like a crescent because it hugs a great bend of the Mississippi — hence 'the Crescent City.' T3: JAZZ was born here, at Congo Square, where enslaved Africans were allowed to gather on Sundays to drum and dance, keeping African rhythms alive that later fused into a wholly new American music. T3: giant screw pumps designed by A. Baldwin Wood (1913) let the city pump itself dry and expand onto drained swamp — the pumps are why New Orleans could grow, and part of why it keeps sinking. T4: the Mississippi is trying to abandon New Orleans — it 'wants' to jump into the Atchafalaya for a shorter, steeper path to the sea, and only the Old River Control Structure upstream keeps it in its channel. T5: the delta is drowning — starved of sediment by upstream levees, coastal Louisiana loses land at a staggering rate, leaving the city ever more exposed.
source: Wikipedia: New Orleans (~half the city at/below sea level, bowl topography, French Quarter on natural levee, Mississippi ~14 ft high-water above sea level, Crescent City bend). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here) then Wikipedia: St. Louis Cemetery / above-ground tombs, Congo Square + Origins of jazz (enslaved Africans, Sunday gatherings), Drainage in New Orleans / A. Baldwin Wood screw pump, Atchafalaya + Old River Control Structure, Louisiana coastal land loss.
framing_note: Wonder voice: every stem names New Orleans or a named place; every answer is a place-fact. Accuracy rail: the below-sea-level bowl and the French-Quarter-on-the-natural-levee are real geography; the above-ground-tombs 'floating coffins' story is the TRADITIONAL/popular explanation (French-Spanish Catholic burial custom also plays a part) — frame it as 'the reason New Orleanians give,' with the tomb-cities themselves as the answer. Stance: celebrate Congo Square honestly — enslaved Africans' music surviving and becoming jazz, born in this PLACE. Dinner-test payoff: the above-ground tomb-cities, and the river straining to jump its course. Lane border: gumbo/beignets/Creole cooking = cooking bank (no food ladder); jazz stays as a place-born cultural creation, not a musician's biography.

name: Teotihuacan
scope: The colossal ancient city of pyramids north of Mexico City. T1: Teotihuacan's Pyramid of the Sun is the third-largest pyramid in the world — a mountain of stone you can climb, behind only Cholula and Giza. T2: a dead-straight boulevard 4 km long runs through the ruins; the Aztecs, finding it centuries later, called it the 'Avenue of the Dead' and named the whole city Teotihuacan, 'the place where the gods were born.' T2: the Aztecs did NOT build it — they discovered it already ancient and abandoned, and who the true builders were is still unknown. T3: at its peak around 500 CE the city held perhaps 100,000+ people — one of the LARGEST cities on Earth at the time, bigger than most cities in Europe. T3: the entire grid is tilted about 15.5 degrees east of north, deliberately aligned to the sky so the sun sets in line with the great avenue on certain days of the year. T4: beneath the Temple of the Feathered Serpent (Quetzalcoatl), archaeologists found a sealed TUNNEL holding pools of liquid mercury and walls that once glittered with mica — a symbolic underworld built under the pyramid.
source: Wikipedia: Teotihuacan (Pyramid of the Sun third-largest pyramid ~65 m, Avenue of the Dead ~4 km, Aztecs found it in ruins and named it 'birthplace of the gods,' builders uncertain, peak population ~100,000-200,000 c.400-500 CE, astronomical grid alignment, sealed tunnel under Temple of the Feathered Serpent with mercury/mica/pyrite). Build stage: corroborate the ~15.5-degree alignment figure and 3rd-largest-by-volume ranking on Grokipedia first.
framing_note: Stance: celebrate Teotihuacan as a full urban CIVILIZATION — a planned metropolis with astronomy and engineering — never 'primitive,' 'lost,' or 'exotic.' Every stem names Teotihuacan or a named structure; every answer is a place-fact. Accuracy rail: the Pyramid of the Sun is third-largest by VOLUME (Cholula and Giza larger); the builders' identity is genuinely unknown, so the answer must say so rather than guess a people. Dinner-test payoff: the Aztecs arriving to find a giant city already ancient — and to this day nobody knows who built it. Lane border: none (pure place/archaeology).

name: Washington, D.C.
scope: The capital city designed whole on paper before it was built. T1: Washington DC was planned on purpose — Pierre L'Enfant (1791) laid grand diagonal AVENUES over a grid, with traffic circles and a long green Mall, one of the first cities in the world designed complete before construction. T2: the Washington Monument visibly CHANGES COLOR partway up — the marble is a different shade because building stopped for over 20 years (money ran out, then the Civil War) and the second batch of stone came from a different quarry. T2: that obelisk is the tallest stone structure in the world and the tallest true obelisk, 555 ft, and was the tallest building on Earth for five years until the Eiffel Tower passed it. T3: the National Mall is an AXIS — the Capitol, the Washington Monument, and the Lincoln Memorial line up in a deliberate sightline nearly 3 km long. T3: by law no ordinary building may rise far above the Capitol — the Height of Buildings Act keeps DC low and horizontal, which is why it has essentially no skyscrapers. T4: much of the monumental core — the western Mall, the Tidal Basin, the ground under the Lincoln Memorial — is RECLAIMED land, dredged and filled out of the Potomac's tidal flats and marsh.
source: Wikipedia: Washington Monument (marble shade changes from 1854 funding halt + Civil War, resumed 1879 with different quarry; 555 ft; tallest structure 1884-1889 until Eiffel Tower; tallest obelisk of stacked stone; L'Enfant plan intended location moved for unstable ground). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here) then Wikipedia: L'Enfant Plan (1791 diagonal avenues over grid), National Mall axis, Height of Buildings Act of 1910, land reclamation of the tidal flats / Potomac Flats.
framing_note: Wonder voice: every stem names Washington DC or a named landmark; every answer is a place/design fact, never a bare politician or date. Accuracy rail: the monument actually shows more than one break/shade — frame the answer as 'the color changes because construction stopped for decades,' which is the true and memorable core; L'Enfant designed the plan but was dismissed, so keep the answer the PLAN, not his biography. Dinner-test payoff: the monument's visible color line, a scar recording a 20-year pause. Lane border: the politics of founding the capital = history bank — stay on the designed city and its landmarks.
history_overlap: The 1790 Residence Act compromise that placed the capital on the Potomac is a history-bank episode; keep answers on the designed city and its landmarks, not the political deal.

name: Quebec City
scope: The clifftop walled city on the St. Lawrence. T1: Quebec City is the ONLY city in North America north of Mexico that still has its old defensive walls all the way around — you can walk the ramparts of a genuine walled city (about 4.6 km of them). T2: it was founded in 1608 by Samuel de Champlain atop a high cliff, Cap Diamant, above the river — a natural fortress. T2: the name 'Quebec' comes from an Algonquin word meaning 'where the river NARROWS' — right here the wide St. Lawrence pinches tight, so whoever held the cliff controlled the gateway to the whole continent's interior. T3: the star-shaped Citadelle, a fortress still garrisoned today, crowns the cliff — its angled bastions were designed so no attacker could approach a wall without being caught in crossfire. T3: the Chateau Frontenac hotel towering over the old town is often called the most photographed hotel in the world — a fairy-tale castle built by a railway company.
source: Wikipedia: Ramparts of Quebec City ('Old Quebec is the only intact example of a fortified walled colonial settlement in North America north of Mexico,' ramparts ~4.6 km, rebuilt 1745, saved by Lord Dufferin), Old Quebec (Champlain 1608, Cap Diamant, Chateau Frontenac, UNESCO 1985) + UNESCO WHC listing 300. Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here); verify the 'Kebec = where the river narrows' etymology and the star-fort Citadelle crossfire design.
framing_note: Wonder voice: every stem names Quebec City or a named place; every answer is a place-fact. Accuracy rail: 'the only walled city in North America north of Mexico with intact ramparts' is the standard sourced claim (Parks Canada / UNESCO); teach 'star fort / bastion' before leaning on it. Dinner-test payoff: the last intact walled city on the continent north of Mexico. Lane border: the 1759 battle is history (below), poutine = cooking bank — frame the cliff and the river-narrows as timeless geography.
history_overlap: The 1759 Battle of the Plains of Abraham is a history-bank episode; frame the cliff and the river-narrows as timeless geography (why the site is a fortress), not the battle.

name: Montreal
scope: The island city named for the green hill at its heart. T1: Montreal is named after Mount Royal (Mont Real), the forested hill rising out of the middle of the city — its park was designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, the same man who made Central Park. T2: Mount Royal LOOKS like an old volcano but isn't — it's the hard, eroded root of an ancient magma INTRUSION, one of the Monteregian Hills; the softer rock around it wore away and left the tough core standing. T2: the whole city sits on an ISLAND in the St. Lawrence River — the Island of Montreal. T3: because winters are brutal, Montreal built the 'Underground City' (RESO), over 30 km of climate-controlled tunnels linking malls, metro, and offices — one of the largest underground pedestrian networks in the world. T3: the city grew right at the Lachine RAPIDS — boats could not pass them, so everyone had to stop and portage here, which made Montreal the great hinge of the fur trade.
source: Wikipedia: Mount Royal (eroded igneous intrusion / Monteregian Hills, NOT a volcano; Olmsted park inaugurated 1876; name from 'Mont Real'; Colline de la Croix 233 m). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here); verify Montreal on the Island of Montreal, the RESO / Underground City length, and the Lachine Rapids / head-of-navigation fur-trade role.
framing_note: Wonder voice: every stem names Montreal / Mount Royal / a named place; every answer is a place-fact. Accuracy rail: correct the volcano MYTH plainly — Mount Royal is an eroded intrusion (a Monteregian Hill), not an old crater; teach the intrusion-vs-volcano distinction; Olmsted's park opened 1876. Dinner-test payoff: the 'volcano' that never erupted, and the vast underground winter city. Lane border: poutine/bagels = cooking bank — keep answers to the PLACE.

name: Havana
scope: The Spanish colonial port on a narrow-necked Caribbean harbor. T1: Havana's Malecon is an 8 km sea-wall and promenade along the Atlantic; in winter cold fronts the waves explode clear over the wall and flood the road. T2: Old Havana (Habana Vieja) is the largest and best-preserved Spanish colonial old town in the Americas — a whole 16th-century city of plazas and stone, still lived in today. T2: the harbor mouth is a narrow bottleneck guarded by the great stone castle El Morro, and a heavy CHAIN was once stretched across the entrance each night to seal the port against pirates. T3: every night at nine o'clock a cannon is fired at the fortress (el canonazo de las nueve) — a 300-year-old ritual that once signaled the closing of the city gates and the raising of that harbor chain. T3: Havana was the assembly point for Spain's TREASURE FLEET — silver from across the Americas gathered in this one harbor before the guarded crossing to Europe, which is why it was fortified like a treasure chest. T4: the city owes everything to its shape — a narrow neck opening into a wide, sheltered pocket bay, the ideal natural harbor that made Havana the key to the Spanish New World.
source: Wikipedia: Malecon, Havana (8 km, construction begun 1901, waves crash over during frentes frios, runs from Old Havana past Centro and Vedado to the Almendares). Dinner-test payoff: the chain stretched across the harbor each night and the cannon still fired at nine. name: Cartagena de Indias
scope: The walled Spanish fortress-city on the Colombian Caribbean. T1: Cartagena is a walled city — about 11 km of massive stone ramparts, 'Las Murallas,' ring the old town, thick enough to walk and gather on. T2: above the city looms Castillo San Felipe de Barajas, the greatest fortress the Spanish ever built in the Americas — honeycombed with TUNNELS so defenders could move unseen and even hear attackers digging. T2: all that stone exists because Cartagena was Spain's treasure vault on the Caribbean — and pirates came for it; Francis Drake seized and ransomed the city in 1586. T3: in 1741 a British fleet of nearly 200 ships and some 25,000 men besieged Cartagena and was BEATEN by a garrison a tenth its size, led by Blas de Lezo, a commander already missing an eye, an arm, and a leg from earlier battles. T3: the Spanish blocked the main harbor mouth, Bocagrande, by sinking ships and building an underwater wall, funneling every attacker through the narrow Bocachica channel straight under the guns of the forts. T4: Cartagena was founded in 1533 and became one of the largest SLAVE markets in the Americas — enslaved Africans were bought and sold in its plazas, and the same walls that guarded silver guarded that trade.
source: Wikipedia: Cartagena, Colombia (11 km walls built 1614-1796; Castillo San Felipe de Barajas 'one of the greatest fortresses built by the Spaniards,' tunnels/galleries; founded 1 June 1533 by Pedro de Heredia; Drake 1586 attack; 1741 siege, Blas de Lezo's ~2,800 defeating Vernon's ~23,600; UNESCO 1984; major slave market at Plaza de los Coches). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here); verify 'largest Spanish fort in the New World' phrasing, Blas de Lezo's specific wounds, and the Bocagrande/Bocachica harbor-blocking defense.
framing_note: Stance: celebrate the Age-of-Discovery ENGINEERING (the fortress-city) honestly, and state plainly, without warping, that Cartagena was a major slave market — both are true and both belong. Every stem names Cartagena or a named fortification; every answer is a place-fact. Dinner-test payoff: the half-a-man admiral who beat a fleet of 200 ships. Lane border: the sieges are battle-history (below) — keep every answer the PLACE (the walls, the fort's tunnels, the harbor defense), not a battle recap.
